verses.15:1: And at once in the morning, the chief priests, having taken counsel with the elders and scribes and the entire council, bound Jesus, led Him away, and delivered Him over to Pilate.
verses.15:2: And Pilate questioned Him, "Are You the King of the Jews?" And answering, He said to him, "You say so."
verses.15:3: And the chief priests were accusing Him of many things.
verses.15:4: Then Pilate questioned Him again, saying, "Do You give no answer? Behold, how many accusations they bring against You."
verses.15:5: Yet Jesus answered nothing further, so that Pilate marveled.
verses.15:6: Now at the feast he was accustomed to release for them one prisoner, whom they asked for.
verses.15:7: And there was one called Barabbas, bound with the insurrectionists who had committed murder during the uprising.
verses.15:8: And the multitude, coming up, began to ask him to do just as he used to do for them.
verses.15:9: And Pilate answered them, saying, "Do you wish that I release for you the King of the Jews?"
verses.15:10: For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered Him over.
verses.15:11: But the chief priests stirred up the multitude that he might release Barabbas for them instead.
verses.15:12: And Pilate answered again and said to them, "What then shall I do with Him whom you call the King of the Jews?"
verses.15:13: And again they cried out, "Crucify Him!"
verses.15:14: Then Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has He done?" Yet they cried out all the more vehemently, "Crucify Him!"
verses.15:15: So Pilate, desiring to satisfy the multitude, released Barabbas to them; and having scourged Jesus, he delivered Him over to be crucified.
verses.15:16: Then the soldiers led Him away inside the courtyard, which is the Praetorium, and summoned together the entire cohort.
verses.15:17: And they dressed Him in purple, and having woven a crown of thorns, they placed it upon Him.
verses.15:18: And they began to greet Him, "Hail, King of the Jews!"
verses.15:19: And they kept striking His head with a reed and spitting upon Him, and kneeling down they paid Him homage.
verses.15:20: And when they had mocked Him, they stripped the purple from Him and clothed Him in His own garments. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.
verses.15:21: And they pressed into service a certain passerby, Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry His cross.
verses.15:22: And they brought Him to the place Golgotha, which, being interpreted, is Place of a Skull.
verses.15:23: And they offered Him wine mingled with myrrh, yet He did not take it.
verses.15:24: And having crucified Him, they divided His garments among themselves, casting lots over them to decide what each should take.
verses.15:25: And it was the third hour when they crucified Him.
verses.15:26: And the inscription of the charge against Him was written: "The King of the Jews."
verses.15:27: And with Him they crucified two robbers, one at His right hand and one at His left.
verses.15:29: And those who were passing by reviled Him, shaking their heads and saying, "Ha! You who tear down the temple and build it in three days,
verses.15:30: save Yourself by coming down from the cross!"
verses.15:31: In like manner the chief priests also, mocking among themselves together with the scribes, were saying, "Others He saved, yet Himself He cannot save.
verses.15:32: Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe!" And those who were crucified with Him also reproached Him.
verses.15:33: And when the sixth hour arrived, darkness came over the entire land until the ninth hour.
verses.15:34: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a great voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which, being interpreted, means, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
verses.15:35: And some of those standing near, upon hearing it, said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah!"
verses.15:36: And someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it upon a reed, and offered it to Him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah is coming to take Him down."
verses.15:37: Then Jesus uttered a great cry and breathed His last.
verses.15:38: And the veil of the sanctuary was torn in two from the top to the bottom.
verses.15:39: Now when the centurion, who stood facing Him, saw that He breathed His last in this manner, he said, "Truly this Man was the Son of God!"
verses.15:40: There were also women watching from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,
verses.15:41: who used to follow Him and minister to Him when He was in Galilee, along with many other women who had come up with Him to Jerusalem.
verses.15:42: And when evening had already come, since it was the Day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
verses.15:43: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was himself awaiting the kingdom of God, came, summoned courage, went in to Pilate, and requested the body of Jesus.
verses.15:44: And Pilate marveled that He should already be dead; and calling the centurion to himself, he inquired of him whether He had been dead for some time.
verses.15:45: And upon learning it from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verses.15:46: And having bought a linen shroud, he took Him down, wrapped Him in the linen, and laid Him in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock; and he rolled a stone against the door of the tomb.
verses.15:47: And Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where He was laid.
verses.16:1: And when the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought aromatic spices, so that they might come and anoint Him.
verses.16:2: And very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb after the sun had risen.
verses.16:3: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away for us the stone from the door of the tomb?"
verses.16:4: And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back, for it was exceedingly large.
verses.16:5: And upon entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, arrayed in a white robe; and they were greatly alarmed.
verses.16:6: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; He is not here. Behold the place where they laid Him.
verses.16:7: But go, tell His disciples and Peter that He is going before you into Galilee; there you shall see Him, just as He told you."
verses.16:8: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them; and they spoke nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verses.16:9: ⟦Now having risen early on the first day of the week, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons.⟧
verses.16:10: ⟦She went and brought word to those who had been with Him, as they were mourning and weeping.⟧
verses.16:11: ⟦Yet when they heard that He was alive and had been seen by her, they disbelieved.⟧
verses.16:12: ⟦And after these things, He appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along on their way into the countryside.⟧
verses.16:13: ⟦And they departed and reported it to the rest, yet they did not believe them either.⟧
verses.16:14: ⟦Afterward He appeared to the eleven themselves as they reclined at table, and He reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw Him after He had been raised.⟧
verses.16:15: ⟦And He said to them, "Go into the entire world and proclaim the gospel to all creation.⟧
verses.16:16: ⟦The one who believes and is baptized shall be saved, but the one who disbelieves shall be condemned.⟧
verses.16:17: ⟦And these signs shall accompany those who believe: in My name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak in new tongues;⟧
verses.16:18: ⟦they shall pick up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it shall by no means harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover."⟧
verses.16:19: ⟦So then the Lord Jesus, after He had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.⟧
verses.16:20: ⟦And they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.⟧

notes.1:1: The phrase "Son of God" is present in the Greek text here and in most manuscripts (including Codex Vaticanus), though it is omitted in Codex Sinaiticus and a few other early witnesses.
notes.1:2: The critical text reads "in Isaiah the prophet," introducing a composite quotation drawn from Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1 (v. 2) together with Isaiah 40:3 (v. 3), named after the prominent prophet Isaiah; later manuscripts harmonize this to "in the prophets."
notes.1:10: The Greek participle translated "torn open" (schizomenous) is a forceful verb of rending, the same verb Mark uses for the tearing of the temple curtain in 15:38.
notes.1:27: Following the punctuation of the Greek source text, "with authority" modifies "He commands"; some editors punctuate the clause to read "A new teaching with authority!"
notes.1:41: Most Greek manuscripts read "moved with compassion" (splanchnistheis), followed here, whereas a few Western witnesses read "moved with indignation" (orgistheis).
notes.2:15: In Greek, "his house" is syntactically ambiguous and may refer either to Levi's house (cf. Luke 5:29) or to Jesus' residence in Capernaum.
notes.2:17: The earliest Greek manuscripts end the verse with "sinners," omitting "to repentance" (which appears in Luke 5:32).
notes.2:19: "Sons of the bridal chamber" renders a Semitic idiom referring to the bridegroom's attendants and wedding guests.
notes.2:26: "In the days of Abiathar the high priest" is much discussed because 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Ahimelech (Abiathar's father) as the priest at Nob; the Greek phrase may denote the broader period of Abiathar's life or the Scripture passage associated with his later prominence as high priest.
notes.3:16: Several important early manuscripts repeat "He appointed the twelve" from verse 14 as a resumptive clause introducing the roster of names.
notes.3:18: "Cananaean" transliterates an Aramaic term meaning "Zealot" (cf. Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13), rather than an inhabitant of Cana or Canaan.
notes.3:21: "His own people" renders a Greek idiom (hoi par' autou) denoting one's relatives or household (cf. v. 31).
notes.3:29: The earliest manuscripts read "an eternal sin" rather than "eternal condemnation" or "eternal judgment."
notes.4:8: The Greek uses a Semitic-influenced distributive idiom (literally "up to thirty, and in sixty, and in a hundred"), conveying multiplicative yields of thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (compare 4:20).
notes.4:11: The critical Greek text reads simply "the mystery of the kingdom of God has been given," without the verb "to know" found in later manuscripts and in the parallels at Matthew 13:11 and Luke 8:10.
notes.4:28: The Greek preserves an unusual colloquial construction in which the adjective "full" stands in the nominative form directly before the accusative noun "grain."
notes.4:39: Literally "Be silent! Be muzzled!" The second command uses the same forceful verb with which Jesus silenced an unclean spirit in Mark 1:25.
notes.5:1: The earliest Greek text reads Gerasenes; later manuscripts harmonize the geography to Gadarenes (cf. Matthew 8:28) or Gergesenes.
notes.5:34: The Greek verb sozo ("has saved you") encompasses both physical healing ("be made well," as in 5:23, 28) and spiritual deliverance.
notes.5:36: The Greek participle parakousas can mean either "disregarding/paying no heed to" or "overhearing"; some later manuscripts instead read akousas ("hearing").
notes.5:41: "Talitha koum" transcribes Aramaic meaning "Little girl, arise"; some later Greek manuscripts spell the imperative koumi.
notes.6:11: The Greek text ends with "as a testimony against them," omitting the later scribal addition comparing the city to Sodom and Gomorrah (harmonized from Matthew 10:15).
notes.6:20: Translates the early Greek reading "was greatly perplexed" (polla eporei), whereas later Byzantine manuscripts read "did many things" (polla epoiei).
notes.6:22: The Greek text reads "his daughter Herodias" (tes thygatros autou Herodiados), an early and difficult reading that many later manuscripts smoothed to "the daughter of Herodias herself."
notes.6:48: The clause "He intended to pass by them" reflects Old Testament theophany language in which God "passes by" to reveal His presence and glory (cf. Exodus 33:19, 22; 1 Kings 19:11).
notes.7:3: The Greek adverb pygme literally means "with the fist," a rare expression denoting a prescribed ritual manner of washing the hands thoroughly.
notes.7:11: Corban is a transliteration of a Hebrew/Aramaic term denoting a gift or offering dedicated to God, which could be vowed so as to withhold material support from one's parents.
notes.7:15: Verse 16 ("If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear") is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is therefore omitted in the Saints Greek Critical Text.
notes.7:19: The masculine participle katharizon ("purifying" or "cleansing") refers back grammatically to Jesus in verse 18, forming Mark's narrative aside that Jesus thereby declared all foods clean.
notes.8:12: The Greek clause literally reads "if a sign shall be given," an elliptical Semitic oath formula expressing an emphatic negation ("by no means shall a sign be given").
notes.8:20: Mark distinguishes between two Greek words for baskets: kophinos (v. 19), a smaller wicker hand-basket, and spyris (vv. 8, 20), a large woven hamper.
notes.8:24: The Greek syntax literally reads "I see the men, because like trees I perceive them walking," vividly reflecting the man's partial, initial restoration of sight.
notes.8:35: The Greek noun psyche can mean either "life" or "soul," creating a deliberate play across vv. 35-37 between earthly life surrendered for Christ and the enduring soul gained or forfeited.
notes.9:23: The Greek definite article before "If You are able" functions as quotation marks echoing the father's plea in verse 22. The earliest manuscripts omit "believe" after "able."
notes.9:29: The earliest manuscripts read simply "by prayer," without the later scribal addition "and fasting."
notes.9:41: Literally "in name, because you are Christ's"; the Greek text omits "My" before "name" and uses the idiom to express belonging to the Messiah as the ground for the kindness shown.
notes.9:48: Alluding to Isaiah 66:24; the earliest manuscripts include this refrain only once here, omitting traditional verses 44 and 46, which repeat it after verses 43 and 45.
notes.9:49: The earliest manuscripts contain only this brief clause, omitting the later addition "and every sacrifice will be salted with salt" (cf. Leviticus 2:13). The imagery evokes testing or purification through trials.
notes.10:7: The Saints Greek Critical Text omits the clause "and be joined to his wife," which enters later manuscripts through assimilation to Genesis 2:24 and Matthew 19:5.
notes.10:21: The critical Greek text omits "take up the cross," a phrase added in later Byzantine witnesses.
notes.10:24: Following the earliest Greek manuscripts, this verse omits "for those who trust in riches," leaving Jesus' statement about entering the kingdom of God unqualified.
notes.10:26: The Greek text reads "to Him" (pros auton) rather than "among themselves" (pros heautous), showing the astonished disciples directing their question straight to Jesus.
notes.10:52: The Greek verb sesoken literally means "has saved" and encompasses both physical restoration ("has made you well") and spiritual deliverance.
notes.11:3: The clause "and He will immediately send it back here" is rendered as part of the disciples' reply, promising that the Lord will promptly return the colt; alternatively, it may be Jesus assuring the disciples that the owner will immediately send it to Him.
notes.11:24: The Greek aorist verb "have received" expresses vivid assurance that the prayer is already granted; some later manuscripts read the present tense "receive."
notes.11:25: Verse twenty-six ("But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses") is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is therefore omitted from the critical text.
notes.11:32: The leaders' deliberation breaks off abruptly without stating the consequence of saying "From men," as Mark intervenes to explain their fear of the multitude.
notes.12:4: "Wounded in the head" translates the rare Greek verb ekephaliosan, found only here in the New Testament; the critical Greek text does not include the later expansion "threw stones at him."
notes.12:26: "In the passage about the bush" (literally "at the bush") reflects the ancient Jewish way of referencing a section of Scripture (Exodus 3) by its main subject prior to chapter and verse numbering.
notes.12:36: "Beneath Your feet" follows the critical text reading hypokato ("beneath/underneath"), whereas Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1) and some later manuscripts read hypopodion ("a footstool").
notes.12:42: A lepton was the smallest Jewish bronze coin in circulation; two lepta equaled one Roman quadrans, the smallest Roman bronze coin (one sixty-fourth of a denarius).
notes.13:14: The Greek text pairs the neuter noun 'abomination' with a masculine participle ('standing'), pointing to a personal desecrator ('where he ought not'). Unlike Matthew 24:15, the critical Greek text of Mark does not include 'spoken of by Daniel the prophet.'
notes.13:29: The Greek verb leaves its subject unexpressed and may be rendered either 'He is near' (referring to the Son of Man in verse 26) or 'it is near' (referring to the fulfillment of these events).
notes.13:32: The critical Greek text reads 'that day or hour' and explicitly includes 'nor the Son,' underscoring that knowledge of the appointed time belongs solely to the Father.
notes.13:35: Evening, midnight, the crowing of the rooster, and dawn designate the four Roman watches of the night.
notes.14:3: The rare Greek adjective pistikēs ("genuine") is debated; it is most commonly understood as "genuine" or "pure," though some interpret it as "liquid" or as a botanical loanword denoting a specific variety of nard.
notes.14:22: The Saints Greek Critical Text reads simply "Take; this is My body," omitting "eat," which entered later manuscripts in assimilation to Matthew 26:26.
notes.14:24: The Saints Greek Critical Text reads "My blood of the covenant" without "new," which appears in later manuscripts under the influence of Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25.
notes.14:36: Mark preserves the Aramaic address Abba—an intimate yet reverent term for "Father"—followed immediately by its Greek equivalent ho patēr ("Father").
notes.14:41: The rare impersonal Greek verb apechei ("It is enough!") is debated and draws from commercial usage ("paid in full"), here signifying that the waiting is over and the appointed hour has arrived.
notes.14:68: The Saints Greek Critical Text ends this verse at "into the forecourt," omitting the clause "and a rooster crowed," which appears in a number of other manuscripts.
notes.14:70: The Saints Greek Critical Text omits "and your speech is like theirs," a clause added in later manuscripts in assimilation to Matthew 26:73.
notes.14:72: The Greek participle epibalōn ("as he reflected upon it") is unusually difficult and has also been interpreted as "breaking down" (bursting into tears) or "covering his head."
notes.15:27: Verse 28, which appears in later manuscripts quoting Isaiah 53:12 ('And He was numbered with the transgressors'), is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is omitted from this text.
notes.15:34: Jesus cries out in Aramaic, quoting Psalm 22:1; the critical Greek text preserves the Aramaic transliteration 'lema' ('why') rather than the Hebrew 'lama'.
notes.15:39: The Greek phrase 'huios theou' lacks the definite article and can be rendered either 'the Son of God' or 'a son of God'; within Mark's Gospel (cf. 1:1, 11; 9:7), it functions as the climactic Christological confession.
notes.15:45: Mark shifts from 'soma' ('body') in Joseph's request (v. 43) to 'ptoma' ('corpse') in Pilate's official grant, highlighting the Roman governor's clinical perspective.
notes.16:8: The earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts end the Gospel of Mark at this verse, closing on a stark note of awe and fear.
notes.16:9: Verses 9-20 (the traditional Longer Ending of Mark) are absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and are enclosed in double brackets to mark their distinct textual status.
notes.16:19: The title 'the Lord Jesus' follows the critical Greek text here, whereas some later manuscripts read simply 'the Lord'.
